title: Ἀλεκτρυόνες καὶ πέρδιξ
part: The Cocks and the Partridge (Chambry 21 · Perry 23)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 21 (= Perry 23). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἀλεκτρυόνας τις ἐπὶ τῆς οἰκίας ἔχων, ὡς περιέτυχε πέρδικι τιθασῷ πωλουμένῳ, τοῦτον ἀγοράσας ἐκόμισεν οἴκαδε ὡς συντραφησόμενον.
sentences.tr: Alektryonas tis epi tēs oikias echōn, hōs perietyche perdiki tithasōi pōloumenōi, touton agorasas ekomisen oikade hōs syntraphēsomenon.
sentences.l: A man keeping cocks at his house, when he came upon a tame partridge being sold, having bought it brought it home to be reared together with them.
sentences.i: A man who kept cocks at his house came upon a tame partridge for sale; he bought it and brought it home to be raised along with them.
sentences.n: ὡς with the future participle (συντραφησόμενον) states the purpose in view: he brought it home “to be reared with them.” περιτυγχάνω takes the dative of what one chances upon. Tame partridges were ordinary household birds in Greece, kept as pets and as decoys for hunting, so the purchase is nothing strange.

sentences.t: Τῶν δὲ τυπτόντων αὐτὸν καὶ ἐκδιωκόντων, ὁ πέρδιξ ἐβαρυθύμει, νομίζων διὰ τοῦτο αὐτὸν καταφρονεῖσθαι ὅτι ἀλλόφυλός ἐστι.
sentences.tr: Tōn de typtontōn auton kai ekdiōkontōn, ho perdix ebarythymei, nomizōn dia touto auton kataphroneisthai hoti allophylos esti.
sentences.l: But with them beating him and driving him off, the partridge was heavy-hearted, thinking that he was despised for this reason, that he is of another tribe.
sentences.i: But when they beat him and drove him off, the partridge took it hard, supposing he was despised because he was of another breed.
sentences.n: A genitive absolute with the article and no noun at all (τῶν δὲ τυπτόντων, “them beating”): the cocks are already in view and need not be named again. διὰ τοῦτο … ὅτι announces the reason and then gives it, “for this reason: because…”. καταφρονεῖσθαι is a passive infinitive in indirect statement after νομίζων. ἀλλόφυλος, “of another tribe,” is the standing word for an outsider.

sentences.t: Μικρὸν δὲ διαλιπών, ὡς ἐθεάσατο τοὺς ἀλεκτρυόνας πρὸς ἑαυτοὺς μαχομένους καὶ οὐ πρότερον ἀποστάντας πρὶν ἢ ἀλλήλους αἱμάξαι, ἔφη πρὸς ἑαυτόν· « Ἀλλ’ ἔγωγε οὐκέτι ἄχθομαι ὑπ’ αὐτῶν τυπτόμενος· ὁρῶ γὰρ αὐτοὺς οὐδὲ αὐτῶν ἀπεχομένους. »
sentences.tr: Mikron de dialipōn, hōs etheasato tous alektryonas pros heautous machomenous kai ou proteron apostantas prin ē allēlous haimaxai, ephē pros heauton· « All’ egōge ouketi achthomai hyp’ autōn typtomenos· horō gar autous oude autōn apechomenous. »
sentences.l: But having let a little while pass, when he saw the cocks fighting against one another and not leaving off before they had bloodied one another, he said to himself: « Well, I for my part am no longer vexed at being beaten by them; for I see them not keeping off even from one another. »
sentences.i: But after a little while, when he saw the cocks fighting each other and not breaking off until they had drawn blood, he said to himself: « Well, I no longer mind being beaten by them — I see they do not spare even one another. »
sentences.n: Verbs of seeing take a supplementary participle: ἐθεάσατο … μαχομένους … ἀποστάντας, “saw them fighting … and not breaking off.” ἄχθομαι does the same with what vexes one, τυπτόμενος, “at being beaten.” οὐ πρότερον … πρὶν ἤ is “not sooner … than,” i.e. not until. ἔγωγε is ἐγώ with the emphatic -γε, “I for my part.” Chambry marks speech with the French guillemets « ».

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι ῥᾴδιον φέρουσι τὰς τῶν πέλας ὕβρεις οἱ φρόνιμοι, ὅταν ἴδωσιν αὐτοὺς μηδὲ τῶν οἰκείων ἀπεχομένους.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti rhāidion pherousi tas tōn pelas hybreis hoi phronimoi, hotan idōsin autous mēde tōn oikeiōn apechomenous.
sentences.l: The story shows that the sensible bear easily the insolences of those nearby, whenever they see them keeping off not even from their own.
sentences.i: The story shows that sensible men bear their neighbours' insults lightly, when they see that those neighbours do not spare even their own kind.
sentences.n: The commonest of the closing formulas, ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι. πέλας is an adverb, “near,” pressed into service as a noun by the article: οἱ πέλας, one's neighbours. ῥᾴδιον is an adverbial accusative, “easily.” ὅταν with the subjunctive (ἴδωσιν) states the general case. τῶν οἰκείων, “their own kin,” answers the partridge's αὐτῶν, and ἀπεχομένους is repeated from his line unchanged.
